title: Terraform on Azure -- azurerm provider, state, modules
exp: The exact same Terraform discipline from the Infrastructure track, now targeting Azure resources via the azurerm provider -- remote state, plan-before-apply, and modules all transfer directly, only the resource types change.
pts: The azurerm provider manages Azure resources the same way the aws provider manages AWS resources -- same plan/apply/destroy workflow, same state file concept.

Remote state on Azure typically lives in a Blob Storage container instead of S3, with state locking handled natively by Azure Blob's lease mechanism -- no separate DynamoDB-equivalent table needed, a genuine simplification versus the AWS setup.
Resource Group as a Terraform-managed resource is usually the very first resource defined in an Azure Terraform configuration, since nearly everything else must be created inside one.

Modules work identically in structure and purpose to the AWS modules from the Infrastructure track -- a reusable package of resources (main.tf/variables.tf/outputs.tf), called with a source and input variables.

The grafana Terraform provider works against Azure Managed Grafana exactly as it did against Amazon Managed Grafana -- same resource types (grafana_dashboard, grafana_data_source), just pointed at a different workspace endpoint and auth method.

Drift detection and the plan-before-apply discipline are platform-agnostic Terraform principles -- nothing about this changes when the underlying cloud changes, which is itself worth saying explicitly in an interview to show the concepts, not just the syntax, transferred.
pr: Configure an azurerm remote state backend using Blob Storage, and explain in one sentence why no separate locking table is needed

r: Blob Storage state + native lease lock

qa.q: How does Terraform remote state locking on Azure differ from the AWS S3+DynamoDB pattern?
qa.a: Azure Blob Storage has a native lease mechanism that Terraform's azurerm backend uses directly for state locking -- there's no need for a separate lock table like DynamoDB on AWS. The state file itself still lives in a Storage Account container, but the locking is a built-in capability of Blob Storage rather than requiring a second service, a genuine simplification in the Azure setup compared to AWS.

qa.q: What's the first resource typically defined in an Azure Terraform configuration, and why?
qa.a: The azurerm_resource_group, because nearly every other Azure resource must be created inside a Resource Group -- it's a required parent, not an optional organizational nicety the way tags are on AWS. Defining it first (and referencing its name/location from every subsequent resource) is the natural starting point for any Azure Terraform configuration.
